COMPANY BAHUBALI is considering taking up one of the two projects-Project-A and Project-B. Both the projects having same life require equal investment of ₹ 400 lakhs each. Both are estimated to have almost the same yield. As the company is new to this type of business, the cash flow arising from the projects cannot be estimated with certainty. An attempt was therefore, made to use probability to analyse the pattern of cash flow from other projects during the first year of operations. This pattern is likely to continue during the life of these projects. The results of the analysis are as follows:

| Project A | | Project B | |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Cash flows | Probability | Cash flows | Probability |
| 55 | 0.10 | 45 | 0.10 |
| 65 | 0.20 | 65 | 0.25 |
| 75 | 0.40 | 85 | 0.30 |
| 85 | 0.20 | 105 | 0.25 |
| 95 | 0.10 | 125 | 0.10 |

**You are required to:**

(i) Calculate variance, standard deviation and co-efficient of variation for both the projects.

(ii) determine which of the two projects is riskier?
workbook:cma-final:p14:ch2:q2.explanation_md:
**Project A: (i)**

$$\text{Expected cash flows or Mean value} = 55 \times 0.10 + 65 \times 0.20 + 75 \times 0.40 + 85 \times 0.20 + 95 \times 0.10 = 75$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Variance} &= (55 - 75)^{2} \times 0.10 + (65 - 75)^{2} \times 0.20 + (75 - 75)^{2} \times 0.40 + (85 - 75)^{2} \times 0.20 + (95 - 75)^{2} \times 0.10 \\ &= 40 + 20 + 0 + 20 + 40 = 120\end{aligned}$$

$$\text{Standard deviation } (\sigma) = \sqrt{\text{Variance}} = \sqrt{120} = 10.95$$

$$\text{Coefficient of variation} = \frac{\text{Standard deviation}}{\text{Mean}} = \frac{10.95}{75} = 0.146$$

**Project B:**

$$\text{Expected cash flows or Mean value} = 45 \times 0.10 + 65 \times 0.25 + 85 \times 0.30 + 105 \times 0.25 + 125 \times 0.10 = 85$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Variance} &= (45 - 85)^{2} \times 0.10 + (65 - 85)^{2} \times 0.25 + (85 - 85)^{2} \times 0.30 + (105 - 85)^{2} \times 0.25 + (125 - 85)^{2} \times 0.10 \\ &= 160 + 100 + 0 + 100 + 160 = 520\end{aligned}$$

$$\text{Standard deviation } (\sigma) = \sqrt{\text{Variance}} = \sqrt{520} = 22.80$$

$$\text{Coefficient of variation} = \frac{\text{Standard deviation}}{\text{Mean}} = \frac{22.80}{85} = 0.268$$

(ii) Project B is riskier as it has higher coefficient of variation.

workbook:cma-final:p14:ch2:q3.explanation_md:
Here, the decision should be taken on the basis of co-efficient of variation. The project with lower co-efficient of variation is less risky.

$$\text{(a) Co-efficient of variation} = \frac{\text{Standard deviation}}{\text{Mean}} \times 100$$

$$\text{Project P: Co-efficient of variation} = \frac{32{,}500}{75{,}000} \times 100 = 43.33\%$$

$$\text{Project Q: Co-efficient of variation} = \frac{36{,}000}{75{,}000} \times 100 = 48\%$$

**Recommendation:** Project P is less risky.

$$\text{(b) Project P: Co-efficient of variation} = \frac{32{,}500}{90{,}000} \times 100 = 36.11\%$$

$$\text{Project Q: Co-efficient of variation} = \frac{36{,}000}{1{,}10{,}000} \times 100 = 32.73\%$$

**Recommendation:** Project Q is less risky.

$$\text{i.e.,}\quad \frac{1}{35} \times \frac{14 \times (1+g)}{0.15 - g} = 10$$

MAHAPRABHU SREECHAITANYA LTD. gives the following information relating to stocks L and M for the past two years:

Rate of Return (%)

| Years | Stock L | Stock M |
|---|---|---|
| 2009-10 | 12 | 14 |
| 2010-11 | 18 | 12 |

a) What is the expected return on portfolio made up of 60% of L and 40% of M?

d) What is the portfolio risk of a portfolio made up of 60% of L and 40% of M?
workbook:cma-final:p14:ch6:q6.explanation_md:
$$\text{(a) Expected rate of return} = E(R) = \frac{\sum R}{n}\text{,}$$

where, $R$ is the rate of return and $n = \text{Number of observations}$

$$\begin{aligned}E(R_L) &= \frac{12 + 18}{2} = 15, \\ E(R_M) &= \frac{14 + 12}{2} = 13, \\ \text{Expected return of portfolio } E(R_P) &= 0.60 \times 15 + 0.40 \times 13 = 14.2.\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{(b) Standard deviation of stock}\quad \sigma &= \sqrt{\frac{\sum [R - E(R)]^{2}}{n}} \\ \sigma_L &= \sqrt{\frac{(12 - 15)^{2} + (18 - 15)^{2}}{2}} = 3 \\ \sigma_M &= \sqrt{\frac{(14 - 13)^{2} + (12 - 13)^{2}}{2}} = 1\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{(c) Covariance between Stock L and Stock M}\quad \text{Cov}_{L,M} &= \sqrt{\frac{\sum [R_L - E(R_L)] \times [R_M - E(R_M)]}{2}} \\ &= \frac{(12 - 15)(14 - 13) + (18 - 15)(12 - 13)}{2} = -3\end{aligned}$$

$$\text{Correlation co-efficient} = r_{L,M} = \frac{\text{Cov}_{L,M}}{\sigma_L . \sigma_M} = \frac{-3}{3 \times 1} = -1.$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text{(d) Portfolio risk}\quad \sigma_P = \sqrt{(P_{L})^{2}(\sigma_{L})^{2} + (P_{M})^{2}(\sigma_{M})^{2} + 2.P_{L}.P_{M}.\sigma_{L}.\sigma_{M}.r_{L,M}} \\ &= \sqrt{(0.6)^{2} \times (0.6)^{2} + (0.6)^{2} \times (0.6)^{2} + 2 \times (0.6)(0.4) \times (3) \times (1) \times (-1)} \\ &= 1.4\end{aligned}$$

workbook:cma-final:p14:ch8:q18.explanation_md:
$C = \text{Current price} = \text{₹ }415$

$S = \text{Strike price} = \text{₹ }400$;

$r = \text{CCRRI} = 0.05$;

$\sigma = 0.22$;

$n = 0.25$ years.

$$\text{P.V. of strike price} = S.e^{-rn} = \text{₹ }400 \times e^{-0.05 \times (3/12)} = \text{₹ }395.$$

$$d_{1} = \frac{\left(\ln\frac{C}{S}\right) + \left(r + 0.5\sigma^{2}\right)n}{\sigma.\sqrt{n}} = 0.5; \qquad d_{2} = d_{1} - \sigma\sqrt{n} = 0.39.$$

$N(d_{1}) = P(Z < 0.5) = 0.5 + 0.1915 = 0.6915$. [From Normal Distribution Table]

$N(d_{2}) = P(Z < 0.39) = 0.5 + 0.1517 = 0.6517$.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Value of call} &= N(d_{1}) \times \text{Current price} - N(d_{2}) \times \text{Present value of strike price.} \\ &= 0.6915 \times 415 - 0.6517 \times 395 = \text{₹ }29.55.\end{aligned}$$

**Put-call Parity Theorem:**

$$\text{Value of Call option} + \text{P.V. of strike price} = \text{Value of Put option} + \text{Current price.}$$

$$\text{Value of Put option} = 29.55 + 395 - 415 = \text{₹ }9.55.$$

Given Spot Exchange rate \$ 1 = FF 7.05, compute the following missing items:

| Forward Dollar premium | B | 6.3% | F |
workbook:cma-final:p14:ch9:q11.explanation_md:
Here, we assume that FF is home currency and US\$ is foreign currency.

$$\text{As per Interest Rate Parity theorem, Forward rate} = \text{Spot rate} \times \frac{(1 + I_{h})}{(1 + I_{f})}$$

$$\text{Rate of forward premium} = \frac{F - S}{S} \times \frac{12}{n} \times 100$$

The missing figures have been calculated as follows:

**Computation of A** (3 months)

$$\begin{aligned}F &= S \times \frac{(1 + r_{h})}{(1 + r_{f})} \\ &= 7.05 \times \frac{\left(1 + \frac{0.195}{4}\right)}{\left(1 + \frac{0.115}{4}\right)} = \mathbf{7.1871}\end{aligned}$$

**Computation of B** (3 months)

Since, forward rate > spot rate, the forward rate is at a premium.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Rate of forward premium} &= \frac{F - S}{S} \times \frac{12}{n} \times 100 \\ &= \frac{(7.1871 - 7.05)}{7.05} \times \frac{12}{3} \times 100 \\ &= \mathbf{7.78\%.}\end{aligned}$$

**Computation of D** (6 months)

$$\frac{D - 7.05}{7.05} \times \frac{12}{6} \times 100 = 6.3$$

$$D = \frac{6.3 \times 7.05 \times 6}{12 \times 100} + 7.05 = \mathbf{7.27.}$$

**Computation of C** (6 months)

$$F = S \times \frac{(1 + r_{h})}{(1 + r_{f})}$$

$$\left(1 + \frac{C}{2}\right) = \frac{7.27}{7.05} \times \left(1 + \frac{0.1225}{2}\right)$$

Solving $\mathbf{C = 18.87\%.}$

**Computation of E** (1 year)

$$F = S \times \frac{(1 + r_{h})}{(1 + r_{f})}$$

$$(1 + r_{f}) = \frac{7.05 \times (1 + 0.20)}{7.52} = 1.125$$

$$\mathbf{E} = r_{f} = \mathbf{0.125}\text{ i.e. }\mathbf{12.50\%.}$$

**Computation of F** (1 year)

As F > S, the forward rate is at premium.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Rate of premium} &= \frac{F - S}{S} \times \frac{12}{n} \times 100 \\ &= \frac{7.52 - 7.05}{7.05} \times \frac{12}{12} \times 100 \\ &= \mathbf{6.67\%.}\end{aligned}$$

workbook:cma-final:p14:ch9:q13.explanation_md:
As the 3-month forward rate is more than the spot rate, it implies that the dollar is at premium.

$$\text{Premium} = [(62.60 - 62.10)/62.10] \times (12/3) \times 100 = 3.22\%$$

Interest rate differential = $11\% - 6\% = 5\% > 3.22\%$. Thus, arbitrage gain possibilities exist. An arbitrageur can take the following steps to make some arbitrage gain:

(i) He borrows ₹ 120,00,000 in Indian rupees @ 6% p.a. for 3 months and converts the same into USD to receive $\text{\textdollar}\,(120{,}00{,}000 \div 62.10) = \text{\textdollar}\,1{,}93{,}236.715$.
(ii) He invests the same amount in USA @11% for 3 months (in the money market).

After 3 months:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{(iii) Total sum available after 3 months} &= \text{\textdollar} 1{,}93{,}236.715 + \text{\textdollar}(1{,}93{,}236.715 \times 11\% \times 3/12) \\ &= \text{\textdollar}\,1{,}98{,}550.715\end{aligned}$$

(iv) He will sell the above USD at the forward rate of ₹ 62.60 and get ₹ 124,29,275.
(v) He will repay $\text{₹ }(120{,}00{,}000 + 120{,}00{,}000 \times 6\% \times 3 / 12) = \text{₹ }121{,}80{,}000$.
(vi) His arbitrage gain = $\text{₹ }(124{,}29{,}275 - 121{,}80{,}000) = \text{₹ }2{,}49{,}275$.
